Why intellectual-property rights sometimes overlap

A commercial product may contain original artistic expression, distinctive branding and an industrially applied decorative design. These features are related in the physical product but may be governed by different legal rules.

The correct legal classification depends on what is being protected and how it is used.

For example, a company might commission an original floral drawing and subsequently apply that drawing to hundreds of commercially manufactured fabric products. The original drawing raises copyright questions, while its industrial application may raise questions under the Designs Act and Section 15 of the Copyright Act.

Section 15 of the Copyright Act: Copyright and industrial designs

Section 15 contains an important rule intended to address the relationship between ordinary copyright and industrial-design protection.

Registered designs

Under Section 15(1), copyright under the Copyright Act does not subsist in a design that is registered under the Designs Act, 2000.

The registered-design proprietor instead relies on the relevant rights granted by the Designs Act for the registered design.

Designs capable of registration but not registered

Section 15(2) addresses a design that is capable of being registered under the Designs Act but has not been registered.

For such a design, copyright under the Copyright Act ceases as soon as an article to which that design has been applied has been reproduced more than 50 times by an industrial process by the copyright owner or another person acting with the owner's licence.

The more-than-50-reproductions rule applies only where the statutory conditions are met. It is not a general rule that every drawing or artistic work loses copyright when 51 copies are made.

Applying the rule

Suppose an artist creates a new decorative pattern capable of registration as an industrial design. The artist does not register it, but authorises a manufacturer to apply it industrially to 60 articles.

If the design satisfies the remaining conditions of Section 15(2), copyright under the Copyright Act ceases in that design once the statutory reproduction threshold is crossed.

By contrast, an independently protected artistic work that does not fall within the statutory definition of a registrable design is not automatically governed by the same cessation rule merely because copies exist.

Can a product shape also function as a trademark?

Certain product shapes or packaging features may function as trademarks if they meet the applicable distinctiveness and other registration requirements.

However, trademark law does not allow every product shape to be registered.

Section 9(3) of the Trade Marks Act excludes marks consisting exclusively of:

  • The shape resulting from the nature of the goods themselves.
  • The shape necessary to obtain a technical result.
  • The shape giving substantial value to the goods.

A shape that qualifies as a registered industrial design therefore does not automatically qualify as a registered trademark. The two statutes apply different legal tests.

Trademark protection and geographical identity

A business trademark primarily distinguishes the commercial source of goods or services. A geographical indication, by contrast, concerns qualifying goods whose relevant quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to geographical origin.

The distinction matters when considering traditional products from Gujarat. A producer's individual business name, an association's collective mark and a geographical indication are not interchangeable legal categories.

Similarly, traditional craft knowledge is not transformed into a new industrial design merely because a manufacturer adopts it. The design must satisfy the applicable requirements of newness, originality and visual eligibility.

Gujarat's intellectual-property facilitation system

The Gujarat Council on Science and Technology (GUJCOST), under the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology, operates an Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre (IPFC) at Gandhinagar.

The centre was formerly identified as the Patent Information Centre. According to the official GUJCOST description available on 14 November 2026, it supports IP awareness and facilitation for stakeholders including students, researchers, innovators, startups, MSMEs and academic institutions.

Its stated coverage includes patents, copyrights, trademarks, industrial designs and geographical indications.

The centre helps users understand protection and filing processes. It is not a replacement for the statutory registration authorities under the relevant central legislation.

Gujarat's Student Startup and Innovation Policy

Gujarat's Student Startup and Innovation Policy 2.0 (SSIP 2.0) also provides a framework for intellectual-property support to eligible innovators and startups through the state's innovation ecosystem.

As described on the official i-Hub Gujarat website on 14 November 2026, its IP-support arrangements include assistance relating to copyrights, trademarks and industrial designs, subject to programme eligibility and prevailing guidelines.

This is a state-level support mechanism. The legal existence and enforceability of copyright, trademarks and registered designs continue to depend on the applicable central laws.

Applying the correct IP category

Consider a hypothetical Gujarat-based enterprise developing a decorative household product.

  • The independently written product manual may be protected by copyright.
  • A distinctive brand name identifying the enterprise may qualify for trademark protection.
  • A new and eligible ornamental exterior of the manufactured article may qualify for industrial-design registration.
  • An unauthorised imitation of the registered brand may raise infringement or passing-off issues.
  • Unauthorised commercial copying of the registered design may raise piracy issues under the Designs Act.

These legal questions should be examined separately. Protection of one element does not automatically establish protection of every other element.

One-glance revision

For an objective question, first identify whether the disputed subject matter is creative expression, a commercial source identifier or the visual appearance of an article. Then apply the appropriate registration requirement, legal exception and protection period.

Prelims focus

  • Copyright Act, 1957, Section 15(1): ordinary copyright does not subsist in a design registered under the Designs Act.
  • Section 15(2): qualifying unregistered designs lose copyright protection when the statutory threshold of more than 50 industrial reproductions is crossed.
  • Trade Marks Act, 1999, Section 9(3): certain natural, functional or value-conferring product shapes cannot be registered as trademarks.
  • GUJCOST operates the Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre in Gandhinagar.
  • SSIP 2.0 is a Gujarat initiative providing support for eligible student and startup innovation activities, including specified IP assistance.
  • Trap: Registered-design protection, artistic copyright and shape-trademark protection are not legally identical.

[Sources: Copyright Act, 1957, Section 15, Copyright Office; Trade Marks Act, 1999, Section 9(3), Intellectual Property India; Designs Act, 2000, Sections 2, 4 and 11; GUJCOST, Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre (formerly PIC), Government of Gujarat, consulted 14 November 2026; i-Hub Gujarat, Financial Assistance for Intellectual Property Support under SSIP 2.0, programme information consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 1, Crafts Heritage.]

title: Copyright–Design Overlap, Product Shapes and Intellectual Property in Gujarat
